lines: One order came out wrong in the warehouse, and three separate systems were involved in getting it there.
A database change, a Kafka topic, a Spark job folding things together. Every single one of them is logging perfectly, on its own terms.
That last part is exactly the trap. Three perfect logs, kept in three separate places, tell you nothing about which hop between them actually broke.
So think about how you'd actually go find that one broken hop, without grepping three separate clusters by hand for the same order id.
Is it one continuous parent-child chain stretching across all three systems? A shared id you search for in each one? Or something else entirely, called a link?
answer: A parent-child chain can't actually do this. A span only ever gets one parent, and a batch job folding in many Kafka records has many producers behind it, not one.
A shared id gets you partway, but it's still three separate systems to search by hand, which is exactly what you were trying to avoid.
Links are built for precisely this: the one structure that survives a single parent limit, a batch fan-in, and a step that's already nested inside some other span, all three at once.

lines: Before any of that works, you need one thing underneath it: a single way to export every signal, so it ends up wherever it needs to go.
Traces, metrics, logs, a bit of context called baggage. All of it leaves the application the same way, and a separate component called the Collector decides where it actually lands.
That separation is what makes the rest of this topic possible at all.
Here's the part that actually crosses the gap between systems: a short, fixed string called traceparent.
A producer writes it straight into the headers of the Kafka record it's sending, because nothing like an HTTP request exists on that hop to carry it automatically.
The consumer reads those same headers back out on the other side. Same string, same trace, unbroken.
Now try to describe a batch consumer honestly, and a parent-child chain falls apart immediately.
Force five separate producer contexts through one span's parent field, one after another, and watch what actually survives: only the last one you assigned.
Hold those same five as links instead, and every single one makes it through intact. That's the whole reason links exist.
But links aren't free, and this is where it gets interesting at real scale.
A nightly job folds in a million Kafka records in one pass. The tracing library's own default cap on links per span is one hundred twenty-eight.
Almost all of those million producer contexts get dropped from the trace, on purpose, by design, the moment that cap is hit.
One more piece makes a trace from Kafka and a trace from a database actually comparable.
They use the exact same attribute names for things like a destination and a partition.
That shared vocabulary is what lets you query a Kafka span and a database span the same way, instead of learning two different systems' own conventions.
Now follow the record all the way through, honestly, including the one place it actually breaks.
Three of the four hops carry the trace automatically: Kafka, the Spark aggregate, the warehouse write. The fourth, the original database write itself, does not.
The tooling's own documentation says so directly. Skip passing the trace metadata into that one write, and the id is simply gone from there on, not degraded, gone.
Last piece, and it's one people genuinely mix up: this is not the same thing as lineage.
One of these tells you what happened during one execution and how long it took. The other tells you which datasets a job actually read and wrote, for one run.
They share exactly one thing, a run identifier, and nothing else about their shape.
So here's the whole shape of what a trace actually gives you across a pipeline like this.

A header that crosses a hop nothing else would carry it across. Links, exactly where a single parent genuinely can't exist. One real seam, named honestly instead of glossed over. And two separate standards, answering two separate questions.
One more to commit to, because it's the kind of thing that actually trips people up on call.
That same nightly job reads a million Kafka records and writes out a single row. Its consumer span's links are capped at one hundred twenty-eight, same as before.
When someone notices that cap later, does it mean the data for the other producers is wrong, or something else entirely?
answer: The link limit lives in the tracing SDK, not in the data path, so it has no say over what the job actually reads or writes.
The aggregate still folds in every one of those million records exactly as it always did.
What you lose is visibility into where most of those records came from afterward. Not the data. Only the trace's own memory of it.
